newsitem.title: FRANCE: Harvest gathers pace in France's grain belt.
newsitem.headline: Harvest gathers pace in France's grain belt.

text.p: Dry, sunny weather allowed the harvest to make swift progress this week in central France's grain belt, local crop officials said on Friday.
Harvesting is now 45 percent complete for soft wheat, 40 percent for durum, 30 percent for spring barley, and 80 percent for rapeseed. The winter barley crop is now all in, they said.
"The harvest is moving at a brisk pace. We are just hoping there is no rain...but the weekend should be dry," an official for the local ONIC grain office in Orleans said.
Last week ONIC officials said the region was heading for large barley and soft wheat harvests as the crops largely recovered from a dry spell in the spring.
"We are confirming this trend," the official said.
Yields on the the rich soils of the north should be up sharply but May and June rains came too late to help the crops fully recover in the south.

Overall the region's soft wheat yields are expected to jump 5-10 percent over the 6.4 tonnes reached in 1996. Barley yields may rise four percent from 6.16 percent last year, with spring barley faring better than winter barley.
Winter barley yields may rise five percent from 6.5 tonnes last year and spring barley yields six percent from 5.5 tonnes.
Higher yields and sowings could push the soft wheat harvest to some 5.5 million tonnes this year from 4.8 million last year.
The region may harvest 1.45-1.50 million tonnes of barley against 1.23 million last year.
Wet weather in June and early July led to some unwanted wheat germination in the south, raising fears quality could be hit.
But the analyst stressed that it was premature to discuss the quality of the whole crop because the harvest had not yet started in the north.

The north, which includes the Eure et Loire, Loir et Cher and Loiret departments, traditionally contributes 60 percent of the wheat and barley crops. The south is made up of the Indre et Loir, Indre, and Cher departments.
The analyst said initial results in the south showed that the widely used Soisson wheat variety had proved very resilient to germination.

Prospects for the durum wheat crop were still uncertain, but the official predicted yields in line or slightly above the 6.2 tonnes reached last year. Area was expected to decline to 27,000 hectares from 33,000 hectares in 1996. That should drive 1997 durum output down to 180,000 tonnes from 204,000.
